item.title: Stand-up Maths: This random noise won an academy award
item.description: White noise is purely random. So random it does not look natural. Perlin noise is noise which serves as a comprise between randomness and looking natural. Watch this video by standupmaths which explains what Perlin noise is, and why it was awarded an Oscar.

item.title: Two members of our group will give lectures as a part of "Inspired by Science" project
item.description:
Science is best when it is communicated to the general public, as it may inspire both the speaker and their audience. That is the idea behind "Įkvėpti mokslo" ("Inspired by Science"), the open lecture series run by the Energy and Technology Museum (ETM) in Vilnius together with the Vilnius City Council and Vilnius University. Science journalist and writer Goda Raibytė-Aleksa will moderate, helping the audience ask their questions.

The lectures start today (see, ETM website) and will take place on every Wednesday up to the 9th of December. Notably, among diverse group of researchers, there will be two members of our group:

  • On the 11th of November Vygintas Gontis will tell about physics-inspired understanding of Lithuanian economic success.
  • On the 18th of November Aleksejus Kononovicius will give a more general perspective on how physicists see social phenomena.

Both talks are free and open to everyone, and no specific background in physical sciences or social sciences is needed. Bring your curiosity and questions! See you!

item.title: Verhulst model
item.description: Fourteen years ago, in a post on Lotka-Volterra equations, I have briefly mentioned Verhulst's population dynamics model. item.title: Binomial distribution as approximation of Hypergeometric distribution
item.description: The derivations of the hypergeometric and binomial distributions follow the same general strategy. In both cases, we first identify all elementary outcomes that are equally likely, then count how many of those outcomes correspond to the event of interest, namely obtaining exactly \( k \) successes. The main difference lies in what constitutes an elementary outcome.

item.title: Lecture on modeling city growth
item.description:
Yesterday, I gave lecture "What makes human behavior interesting to physicists?" (lt. "Kuo fizikams įdomus žmonių elgesys?") to a large group of high school students participating in a project "Student for a day", organized by Vilnius University.

While I do not teaching anything directly related to my research, I have volunteered to do a special introductory lecture and try to explain why physicists are interested in social systems. Initially, I intended to tell students more-or-less about the same things I did when giving a talk at Nacionalinė moksleivių akademija. Yet instead of simply trimming the lecture, I have decided instead to focus on a single example and develop it a bit more. So, in the end I have talked about how "normal" (Gaussian) humans create cities that are rather "peculiar". This lead me to talk about Malthus and Verhulst models of population growth (dedicated blog post should be published soon) and then pivot to preferential attachment as seen in Simon model (I hope to prepare dedicated blog post early next year).

If you are interested, you can take a sneak peek at my slides here (though they are in Lithuanian).

item.title: Binomial distribution
item.description:
Suppose that a box contains \( N \) balls, of which \( \textcolor{red}{M} \) are red ("success") and \( \textcolor{red}{N-M} \) are of another color ("failure"). We now draw balls with replacement (notably, if we draw without replacement, we would end up with hypergeometric distribution), so that after each draw the selected ball is returned to the box before the next draw. Consequently, each draw is independent, and the probability of success remains constant,

\begin{equation} p=\frac{M}{N}. \end{equation}

Let \( Y \) denote the number of red balls drawn ("successes") in the \( n \) draws ("experiments"). We wish to determine the probability that exactly \( \textcolor{red}{k} \) of the \( n \) (all) draws are successes.

item.title: A more intuitive introduction to probability density functions
item.description: In quite a few statistical physics books, probability density functions (abbr. PDF) are introduced instantaneously by using the Dirac delta function. In my view, this approach is not very intuitive. While reading Heinz's book on mathematical modeling [1], I came across a more intuitive explanation, and I would like to share it here on Physics of Risk.

item.title: Approximating characteristic function of bounded Pareto distribution with α=1
item.description: During the summer, I received an email from a researcher at university abroad inquiring about how we (myself and my senior colleague, prof. B. Kaulakys) derived the approximation for the characteristic function of bounded Pareto distribution (for the particular case with \( \alpha = 1 \)). The approximation was given in [1], but derivation turned out to be somewhat more involved than I remembered. Originally, I derived it with the help of Wolfram Engine, while my colleague consulted various mathematical formula compendiums. Unfortunately, I was unable to find any notes containing the derivation. So I have attempted to reconstruct a combined approach from scratch. You'll find the derivation below.
